title: What did you do yesterday?
goal: Form the past with *hebben* + the past participle, and master the **'t kofschip** spelling rule that decides between -t and -d.
bekal: forming the *voltooid deelwoord*: ge- + stem + t/d
using the 't kofschip rule to choose -t or -d
wave: Go back to **unit 15**: describe five people you know, three sentences each, with correctly inflected adjectives.

dialogs.title: Dialog — Maandagochtend
dialogs.intro: Monday morning in class. The same question as every Monday.

lines.speaker: Sanne:
lines.text: En? Wat heb je dit weekend gedaan?
lines.id: So? What did you do this weekend?
lines.literal: and? what have you this weekend done?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ik heb hard gewerkt aan mijn verslag.
lines.id: I worked hard on my report.
lines.literal: I have hard worked on my report.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Nee. Zaterdag heb ik gefietst naar Amsterdam.
lines.id: No. On Saturday I cycled to Amsterdam.
lines.literal: no. Saturday have I to Amsterdam cycled.

lines.speaker: Sanne:
lines.text: Vanaf Utrecht? Dat is veertig kilometer!
lines.literal: from Utrecht? that is forty kilometers!

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ik heb het gedaan. Mijn benen hebben het gemerkt.
lines.id: I did it. My legs felt it.
lines.literal: I have it done. my legs have it noticed.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ik heb koffie gedronken bij een gracht en foto's gemaakt.
lines.id: I had coffee by a canal and took photos.
lines.literal: I have coffee drunk at a canal and photos made.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ik heb met mijn ouders gebeld. Ze hebben me gemist.
lines.id: I called my parents. They missed me.
lines.literal: I have with my parents called. they have me missed.

lines.speaker: Sanne:
lines.id: Makes sense. Did you get any rest too?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ja — vanochtend, in de trein hierheen.
lines.id: Yes — this morning, on the train here.
lines.literal: yes — this-morning, in the train to-here.

notes: **Wat heb je gedaan?** — the most common past tense in spoken Dutch is the *voltooid tegenwoordige tijd*: *hebben/zijn* + past participle. It looks like the English present perfect ("I have done"), but Dutch uses it where English says "I did" — even with *gisteren*.
**Ik heb hard gewerkt** — note *gewerkt* at the **end of the sentence**. Just like the modal verbs in unit 13, the participle always falls to the very back.
**Zaterdag heb ik gefietst** — the sentence opens with a time expression, so the helper verb (*heb*) is in second position and the subject follows. The unit 10 rule still applies.
**Gedronken** and **gedaan** don't follow the regular pattern — both are strong verbs, waiting for you in unit 18. For now, just memorize them; they're too common to put off.
**Ze hebben me gemist** — from *missen*. The stem ends in *s*, which is in 't kofschip, so the ending is *-t*: *gemist*.
**Heb je uitgerust?** — a separable verb (*uitrusten*) puts *ge-* in the **middle**: uit-**ge**-rust. This form almost always surprises beginners the first time they see it.
**Logisch** is pronounced **LOH-khis** — remember the *-isch* rule in the pronunciation chapter.

grammars.title: Forming the past participle (voltooid deelwoord)
body: For regular verbs, the formula is: **ge-** + stem + **-t** or **-d**.
after: Verbs with a fixed prefix (*be-*, *ge-*, *ver-*, *ont-*, *her-*, *er-*) **don't** take *ge-*: *betaald*, *verteld*, *ontbeten*. Foreign *-eren* verbs do: *studeren* → *gestudeerd*, *proberen* → *geprobeerd*.
Separable verbs slip *ge-* into the middle: *opbellen* → *op**ge**beld*, *uitrusten* → *uit**ge**rust*, *meenemen* → *mee**ge**nomen*.
If the stem already ends in *-t* or *-d*, nothing is added: *zetten* → *gezet*, *praten* → *gepraat*, *antwoorden* → *geantwoord*.

grammars.title: 't Kofschip — choosing -t or -d
body: A memory trick taught in every Dutch school: if the **last sound of the stem** is in the word *'t kofschip*, the ending is **-t**. If not, **-d**.
after: ⚠️ What counts is the **sound**, not the letter in the dictionary form. *Verhuizen* has the stem *verhuis* (a z sound spelled s at the end) — but the original sound is *z*, so the ending is **-d**: *verhuisd*. Likewise *leven* → *geleefd*.
The phrase Dutch schoolchildren use: **'t kofschip** — now often extended to **'t fokschaap** so that the *ch* sound gets in too.
The good news: in speech, a final *-t* and *-d* sound **the same** (see pronunciation: word-final consonants harden). The rule matters for writing; your speaking won't suffer from it.

blocks.text: Notice that **two verbs frame the sentence**: the helper in second position, the main verb at the end. All expressions of time, manner, and place stand in between, in the TMP order from unit 10.

blocks.title: Past time expressions
items: *vorige week* (last week), *vorig jaar* (last year), *vorige maand* (last month).
*net* (just now): *Hij is net weggegaan.* — *pas* (only recently): *Ik ben pas verhuisd.*
*al* (already) and *nog niet* (not yet): *Heb je al gegeten? — Nee, nog niet.*
⚠️ *Een uur geleden* = an hour ago. Like English *ago*, *geleden* always comes **after** the length of time: *twee dagen geleden*.

blocks.text: The last four rows show both exceptions at once: fixed prefixes that drop *ge-* (*betaald*, *verhuisd*, *verteld*), and separable prefixes that slip it in (*opgebeld*, *uitgerust*).

The practice that sticks fastest: take the ten verbs you use most, write their participles, then make one past-tense sentence with each about your own day yesterday. Sentences about yourself stick far better than any textbook example.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the blanks with the past participle (voltooid deelwoord).
Fill in the blanks with -t or -d, following the 't kofschip rule.
Fill in the blanks: put each sentence in the past.

items: What did you do this weekend?

answers: gewerkt — gewoond — gefietst — gebeld — gekookt — gemist — betaald — opgebeld
t — d — t — t — d — t
Ik heb hard gewerkt. — Zij heeft haar moeder gebeld. — Wij hebben naar Amsterdam gefietst. — Hij heeft de rekening betaald. — Ik heb uitgerust.
Wat heb je dit weekend gedaan? — Ik heb hard gewerkt. — Ik heb mijn ouders gebeld. — We hebben een uur gepraat. — Heb je het gehoord? — Ik heb nog niet gegeten.
